stories.headline: Israelis hold final rally against Netanyahu ahead of consequential election
stories.title: Israelis hold final rally against Netanyahu ahead of consequential election
stories.summary: Israelis held a final large rally against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of what has been described as the most consequential election in the country's history. Meanwhile, the death toll rose from Friday's attack on a church in Jordan. And an Iranian military commander said his country will not allow US warships to enter the Persian Gulf as concerns grow of a return to all-out war. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here. The crowd heard calls for a commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry. Netanyahu's chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, attended the

stories.headline: Election observer briefs micro-observers ahead of local body elections
stories.title: Election observer briefs micro-observers ahead of local body elections
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Tirupati: A special training programme for micro-observers was conducted at Tirupati on Saturday to ensure the smooth, transparent, and impartial execution of the upcoming municipal elections within the Tirupati Municipal Corporation limits.
The orientation session was jointly addressed by Election Observer M Varaprasad, District Joint Collector R Govinda Rao, and Tirupati Municipal Corporation Commissioner M Jayakrishna.
The senior officials detailed the duties, responsibilities, and procedural regulations that micro-observers must strictly enforce on polling day.

Directing observers to maintain high vigilance, officials stressed that strict implementation of the State Election Commission’s guidelines is mandatory to ensure complete transparency throughout the election process.
Key polling protocols were outlined, including the restriction that only one authorized polling agent per contesting candidate can be present inside a polling station at any given time.
Officials explained the mandatory procedure for sealing empty ballot boxes in the presence of polling agents before voting commences.

Furthermore, micro-observers were instructed to ensure agents are permitted to record serial numbers of ballot boxes and green paper seals, and inspect marked copies of the electoral roll per regulations.

Reiterating that individuals without valid official entry passes must be denied access to polling booths, the administration emphasized maintaining strict discipline, security, and decorum at all polling stations.
Micro-observers were instructed to monitor every stage of the voting process closely and report any procedural lapses or code violations to high-level officials immediately.

stories.headline: The Trump method
stories.title: The Trump method
stories.summary: India and the United States are talking the language of friendship again, but the question is whether the relationship is becoming more equal or simply more transactional. After months of tariff disputes, disagreements over Russian oil and the controversy surrounding President Donald Trump’s claims of having stopped the India-Pakistan conflict in May 2025, Washington is now signalling that a long-pending trade agreement could finally be within reach. The timing is significant. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India this week, his meetings with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and his outreach to business leaders have revived hopes of a breakthrough. Rubio has described the agreement as “incredibly close”, saying that the two sides are weeks, rather than months, away from finalising it. Trump, too, has said that the countries are “pretty close” to a deal, although he has indicated that it will be different from other agreements Washington has concluded. This is encouraging, but India has heard optimistic signals before. The real test will be the terms of the agreement, not the enthusiasm with which it is announced. Pressure first, partnership later? Trump’s approach to diplomacy is increasingly familiar. He creates pressure through tariffs, public statements and threats, then presents the prospect of a negotiated settlement as an opportunity that the other side should not miss. Last year, the US heavily imposed tariffs on Indian goods, still hurting the business companies, more so when additional tariffs linked to New Delhi’s purchase of Russian oil were imposed. The move definitely affected Indian exporters and created uncertainty among businesses. It also raised questions about the reliability of a strategic partner that had for years encouraged India to strengthen economic, strategic and defence ties with Washington, which India followed dutifully. India should definitely be worried not only about tariffs but also about the uncertainty surrounding the US’s fluctuating decisions or pressure tactics. Any relationship or trade needs trust to plan investments and exports, however difficult the negotiations be. However, if access to the American market can suddenly become a tool to put pressure on India, it naturally raises eyebrows and concerns. The US wants India to be a trusted strategic partner, but its trade policies risk making that partnership appear conditional. In other words, Washington wants India to remain close, but seems keen to ensure that it does so largely on American terms. Trump believes that earlier administrations gave away too much and that even friendly countries should be pressed to offer better commercial terms. During his current visit, Rubio acknowledged in an interview with Network18 that both countries would defend their national interests and that a sustainable agreement must benefit both sides. The outcome is that pressure can produce concessions without necessarily producing trust. Political observers feel that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has chosen not to engage in a public confrontation with Trump. He has continued to engage Washington, while India’s diplomatic establishment has defended the country’s position on trade, energy security and relations with Pakistan. PM Modi perhaps is avoiding a direct clash with the American President. To some extent, it seems, the restraint is deliberate. India has substantial interests in the United States, from defence technology and advanced manufacturing to investment, education and the opportunities available to Indian professionals. A public exchange of accusations between the two leaders might generate headlines but would do little to resolve the underlying disagreements. PM Modi also knows that the United States remains important to India’s wider strategic calculations, particularly in the Indo-Pacific and in managing the challenge posed by China. Allowing a trade dispute to damage cooperation across these areas would be costly. But restraint should not be confused with acceptance. India’s position on strategic autonomy means that it cannot allow another country to dictate its energy choices, regional relationships or security decisions. The challenge for PM Modi is to remain personally measured while ensuring that India’s negotiating position remains firm. There is, however, a political cost to excessive silence. When an American President repeatedly makes claims that conflict with India’s account of important events, New Delhi must ensure that its own position is communicated clearly enough to prevent another country’s version from becoming the accepted international narrative. Trump’s repeated claims of having stopped the India-Pakistan hostilities continue to remain an irritant in bilateral ties. Following the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 people, India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7. The military confrontation ended on May 10, following direct contact between the two countries’ Directors General of Military Operations. Trump, however, in every reference to India or Pakistan, claims credit for stopping the fighting. He goes further, claiming that he threatened to withhold trade benefits. Media reports counted more than 60 such claims by January 2026. India has consistently maintained that the ceasefire understanding was reached directly between the two countries, without US mediation. Prime Minister Narendra Modi also made it clear that no trade deal was discussed in connection with ending the hostilities. For India, the issue is not merely about who takes credit for the ceasefire. It is unnecessarily internationalising the India-Pakistan dispute. Trump’s repeated claim has put Modi and his team in a delicate position. India wants to avoid a confrontation with the US President, while silence could be seen as acceptance of Washington’s version. New Delhi has therefore chosen to maintain its position through official statements while keeping diplomatic channels open. Is a trade deal finally within reach? There are reasons for cautious optimism. During the October 21-23 visit of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to Mumbai and Gujarat, Rubio said the agreement was down to a small number of unresolved issues, including differences over the precise language of the text. Trump has also indicated that a deal is close. These are the clearest recent signals that both governments want to move beyond the prolonged impasse. The negotiations, however, remain difficult so far. Washington has been insisting on greater access to India’s market and has pressed for increased purchases of American energy and technology. India, for its part, continues to protect the interests of domestic producers, especially farmers and exporters while securing competitive terms for its goods in the US market. Agriculture, industrial products, tariff treatment and regulatory differences have all been sensitive areas in the negotiations between the two countries. India cannot afford an agreement that offers headline benefits but imposes disproportionate costs on farmers, smaller manufacturers or other vulnerable sectors. The US, which has recently lifted US sanctions on Russia, linked to purchases of Russian energy, has definitely eased pressure. Rubio, in his recent visit and several of the media interviews, has acknowledged that sanctions and tariffs can have consequences for countries beyond their immediate targets. That recognition matters because India’s energy decisions are shaped by global availability and national requirements, not simply by Washington’s preferences. Yet it is too early to be optimistic. Beyond the trade deal: India-US ties need mutual respect India and the US have strong reasons to remain close partners. Defence cooperation, new technology, semiconductors, maritime security and the Quad bring the two countries together. The large Indian community in America and strong business ties also strengthen the relationship. But friendship between the two countries cannot depend only on common interests or good words. It also requires trust, respect and stability in policies, even when differences arise. The US needs to understand that India will not agree to every American demand. Similarly, India must stand firm on its national interests and maintain its freedom to take independent decisions, while continuing to work with the US. So far, PM Modi has taken a wise decision to avoid direct confrontation with Trump. Many strategic analysts and political observers support this sensible approach. But this restraint must go hand in hand with a firm stand during negotiations. Diplomacy is not about exchanging sharp words in public; it is about protecting national interests and finding solutions. There is fresh hope for a trade deal following Rubio’s positive remarks and Trump’s latest signals. But much will depend on whether both sides are ready to make reasonable compromises without putting pressure on each other. Finally, India-US friendship will be judged not by how often the two leaders call each other friends, but by how much respect they show for each other’s interests, their subjects, when it comes to making difficult decisions. Author is National Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: Op Sindoor proved no target beyond IAF's reach; air power remains India's primary responder: Air Chief Marshal AP Singh
stories.title: Op Sindoor proved no target beyond IAF's reach; air power remains India's primary responder: Air Chief Marshal AP Singh
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 25: The Indian Air Force's calibrated strikes across the Western front during Operation Sindoor -- spanning 1,200 km in breadth and 200 km in depth--demonstrated that no target is beyond its reach, Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal AP Singh said on Sunday, in an apparent warning to Pakistan. In an exclusive interview with PTI, the Air Chief described the operation as a validation of the IAF's capability-centric approach, emphasising that it reaffirmed air power's decisive role as both the nation's primary responder and its strategic deterrent. At the same time, the IAF Chief cautioned that validation of the IAF's approach must not be a reason to "stand still" as the way forward is to deepen and widen this capability across the force. "Operationally, one lesson stands out: we must always retain multiple options and the ability to adapt rapidly as the adversary changes tactics," the Chief of Air Staff who oversaw the four-day operation said. "A capability-centric force is inherently better at this, because it can draw on many tools rather than depend on one. That same flexibility allowed us to calibrate our response and keep control of escalation," he said. Launched in response to the Pahalgam terror attack, Operation Sindoor saw India carry out precision strikes against terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied territories in May last year-- marking the most daring cross-border military action by the country since the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War. "Operation Sindoor proved that the path we have chosen is the right one. We will continue along it with even greater resolve, so that if the nation calls upon us again, the IAF responds more swiftly, more precisely and more decisively, on the nation's terms," he said. The Chief of the Air Staff also noted that some of the indigenously developed weapons systems performed "exceptionally", delivering crippling blows deep into enemy territory, and that the IAF honoured its commitment to "zero collateral damage" throughout the operation. "Operation Sindoor was, above all, a validation of the capability-centric approach the IAF has been pursuing. We have moved from thinking in terms of individual platforms to thinking in terms of capability, where every aircraft, sensor, weapon and network is integrated so that the combined effect is far greater than the sum of the parts," the IAF Chief said. "The operation put that philosophy to the test in real operations, and it delivered. It reaffirmed the decisive role of air power as both the nation's primary responder and its strategic deterrent, and it reinforced the enduring importance of speed, precision, integration and adaptability," he said. The Air Chief Marshal was responding to a question on the IAF's key takeaways from Operation Sindoor across operational tactics, strategic options, setbacks, and firepower. The operation's success did not come from any single weapon or platform. It came from the combined effect of accurate intelligence, networked operations, stand-off and precision weapons, electronic warfare, layered air defence and counter-UAS (Unmanned Aerial Systems) capabilities, all working as one system, he said. "On the offensive side, calibrated targeting across the entire front, spanning 1,200 km in breadth and 200 km in depth, made it clear that no place is beyond the IAF's reach," he said. "Some of our indigenously developed weapons performed exceptionally, delivering crippling blows deep into enemy territory, and we honoured our commitment to zero collateral damage throughout," he said. The Chief of the Air Staff said India's home-grown networked air defence defeated the large number of drones and stand-off weapons launched by the Pakistan military as the nation could act with confidence. "Offence and defence reinforced each other, which is precisely what a capability-centric force is designed to achieve," he said. Air Chief Marshal Singh said Operation Sindoor also demonstrated the value of joint and multi-domain integration, adding bringing together the air, land, maritime, space, cyber and electromagnetic domains enabled faster decision-making and greater operational effect. The IAF Chief, however, said the force must now focus on strengthening combat mass, ISR (intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance) prowess, electronic warfare, counter-UAS capability, resilient networks and AI-enabled decision support. "Equally, we must build the ability to sustain high-intensity operations over time through robust logistics, maintenance, infrastructure and, above all, indigenous production. Work is already under way on each of these fronts. Air Chief Marshal Singh said the IAF's vision is closely aligned with the larger national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, as a developed India must also be a secure and resilient India. "The Defence Forces Vision 2047 likewise envisages an integrated, multi-domain and technologically advanced military in support of this national ambition," he said. For the IAF, the Chief of Air Staff said it means evolving into a multi-domain aerospace force capable of protecting India's growing economic, technological and strategic interests across the entire spectrum of conflict. "We have set out a clear, structured path towards that goal. The IAF's Capability Perspective Plan-2047 lays down long-term priorities based on emerging technologies, and it feeds into ten-year plans that are updated periodically," he said. In the space domain, the Air Chief Marshal said the broader direction is reflected in the IAF Space Vision 2047. "Our emphasis will be on 'Aatmanirbharta', advanced aerospace technologies, artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, space, cyber, precision weapons and resilient networks. Just as important, we will build the industrial ecosystem needed to sustain all of these capabilities," he said. The IAF Chief argued that a secure India creates the environment for economic growth, while a technologically and economically stronger India provides the foundation for greater strategic power. "Realising this vision will require a whole-of-nation approach, and the IAF is committed to playing its full part," he said. "By 2047, we aim to be one of the world's most capable, innovative and technologically self-reliant aerospace forces, a force that stands as both the guardian and a driver of a developed India," he noted.

Air Chief Marshal Singh said the IAF's vision is closely aligned with the larger national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, as a developed India must also be a secure and resilient India.
The Air Chief Marshal was responding to a question on the IAF's key takeaways from Operation Sindoor across operational tactics, strategic options, setbacks, and firepower.

stories.headline: GoI appoints Sajjan Singh Yadav as J&K Chief Secretary
stories.title: GoI appoints Sajjan Singh Yadav as J&K Chief Secretary
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 24: The Government of India on Saturday appointed Sajjan Singh Yadav as the new Chief Secretary of Jammu and Kashmir, replacing Atal Dulloo and ending weeks of speculation over J&K’s top administrative post. The order issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs said that Yadav was transferred from Delhi to Jammu and Kashmir and appointed as Chief Secretary from November 1, 2026, or the date he assumes office. Yadav’s appointment marks a major change in J&K's administrative structure. Yadav becomes the first of the core AGMUT officers to take charge of the J&K administration after the exclusive J&K cadre was abolished in 2021 and merged into the broader AGMUT (Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram, and Union Territories) pool. The decision also ends speculation supporting some other senior candidates in the succession race. Officers currently hold ing positions in J&K belonging to earlier batches and senior to Yadav include Shaleen Kabra of the 1992 batch who is Financial Commissioner and Additional Chief Secretary, Jal Shakti Department; Ashwani Kumar of the 1992 batch, who is Financial Commissioner (ACS), Power Development Department (PDD); Dheeraj Gupta of the 1993 batch who is Additional Chief Secretary to the Chief Minister; Ashish Chandra Verma of the 1994 batch who is Financial Commissioner and Additional Chief Secretary, Agriculture Production Department; Sheilender Kumar of the 1995 batch who is Additional Chief Secretary Finance Department; and Anil Kumar Singh of the 1995 batch who is Additional Chief Secretary Public Works Department (PWD). Apart from them, Bipul Pathak of the 1992 batch, Navin Chowdhary of the 1994 batch, and Rohit Kansal of the 1995 batch, all currently on deputation are also seniors to Yadav. The AGMUT cadre is responsible for Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram, and eight Union Territories: the NCT of Delhi, Puducherry, J&K, Ladakh, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Lakshadweep. Yadav, who is experienced in dealing with the complicated administrative arrangements of Union Territories, held the positions of Additional Chief Secretary and Chief Executive Officer at the Delhi Jal Board. He has done a postgraduate diploma in Public Policy from the Hubert Humphrey School from Minnesota University, a Master’s in Finance from Delhi University, and a Master’s in Economics from Harvard University. The bureaucratic transition takes place at a politically sensitive time in J&K. After years of direct central rule, when an elected assembly was restored, the new Chief Secretary had to deal with a special kind of power-sharing situation. In the present arrangement under the Union Territory system, the Lieutenant Governor, appointed by the Centre, maintains control over important matters like Police, public order, and the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) bureaucracy, while the elected Chief Minister leads the civilian government. The Chief Secretary in J&K is responsible for coordinating the work of the various government departments. The post is essential for putting administrative decisions into effect and for handling the relationship between the bureaucracy, the elected government, and the Lieutenant Governor’s administration. That a senior officer drawn from the wider Union Territory cadre has been appointed to lead J&K bureaucracy is significant at a time when administrative coordination and the allocation of responsibilities between the elected government and the Centre are still politically sensitive. No reason was given in the order issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs for refusing to grant an extension to the outgoing Chief Secretary, Atal Dulloo, a member of the original J&K batch who turned sixty on Saturday and is set to retire on October 31. Dulloo has held the position of Chief Secretary since December 2023. Earlier, it was reported that Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha had suggested a one-year extension for Dulloo. However, the final decision had to be made by the competent authority in charge of approving the appointment and the arrangements for service. Dulloo has left behind an administrative legacy of handling the large-scale security and logistical requirements of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and of J&K’s first Assembly elections in 10 years. However, a rift started between him and the civilian government during his last weeks in office. Dulloo was involved in a row concerning a proposal aimed at restoring J&K’s statehood, a politically sensitive matter. Dulloo and the administration’s Law Secretary had sent a letter to Legislative Assembly Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather to oppose the introduction and discussion of the resolution, citing legal concerns as the reason. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah strongly objected to the intervention, and the action in question aroused criticism from the Members of Parliament as well as leading to a privilege-motion notice being tabled against the officials. The controversy intensified the questions concerning the relationship between the bureaucracy and the elected government led by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, which came into office in 2024 after a period of direct administration by the central government. Although the Government of India has not officially confirmed that the dispute over statehood was the reason why the government rejected Dulloo’s extension, the fact that the transition has taken place shows that administrative control in J&K is still being readjusted. It also raises questions regarding Dulloo’s next task. According to reports, Dulloo is being considered for the post of Chairman of the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission, which currently has no chairman. However, there has not been any official announcement regarding the matter.

stories.headline: Operation Trident: Rs 100 cr hawala transactions exposed, 18 arrested in drug crackdown
stories.title: Operation Trident: Rs 100 cr hawala transactions exposed, 18 arrested in drug crackdown
stories.summary: Union home minister Amit Shah announced Operation Trident, which targeted an international narcotics cartel in India. The operation, conducted in Assam, Mizoram, and Manipur, uncovered significant hawala transactions and led to arrests. Authorities froze numerous bank accounts and seized illegal items, including detonators and cash. Shah emphasized the government's commitment to eradicating drug networks by December 31, 2029.
